{{Short description|Type of composite number with an even number of digits}}
In [[recreational mathematics]], a '''vampire number''' (or '''true vampire number''') is a [[composite number|composite]] [[natural number]] with an even number of [[numerical digit|digits]], that can be factored into two natural numbers each with half as many digits as the original number, where the two factors contain precisely all the digits of the original number, in any order, counting multiplicity. The two factors cannot both have trailing zeroes. The first vampire number is 1260 = 21 × 60.<ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=VampireNumber|title=Vampire Numbers}}</ref><ref name="jandersen">{{cite web |last1=Andersen |first1=Jens K. |title=Vampire numbers |url=http://primerecords.dk/vampires/}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>N</math> be a natural number with <math>2k</math> digits:

:<math>N = {n_{2k}}{n_{2k-1}}...{n_1}</math>

Then <math>N</math> is a vampire number if and only if there exist two natural numbers <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, each with <math>k</math> digits:

:<math>A = {a_k}{a_{k-1}}...{a_1}</math>
:<math>B = {b_k}{b_{k-1}}...{b_1}</math>

such that <math>A \times B = N</math>, <math>a_1</math> and <math>b_1</math> are not both zero, and the <math>2k</math> digits of the [[concatenation]] of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> <math>({a_k}{a_{k-1}}...{a_2}{a_1}{b_k}{b_{k-1}}...{b_2}{b_1})</math> are a [[permutation]] of the <math>2k</math> digits of <math>N</math>. The two numbers <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are called the ''fangs'' of <math>N</math>.

Vampire numbers were first described in a 1994 post by [[Clifford A. Pickover]] to the [[Usenet]] group sci.math,<ref>[http://groups.google.com/group/sci.math/msg/f17b2281a4aa16da?lr=&ie=UTF-8 Pickover's original post describing vampire numbers]</ref> and the article he later wrote was published in chapter 30 of his book ''Keys to Infinity''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pickover |first1=Clifford A. |title=Keys to Infinity |date=1995 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=0-471-19334-8}}</ref>

== Examples ==

|-

1260 is a vampire number, with 21 and 60 as fangs, since 21 × 60 = 1260 and the digits of the concatenation of the two factors (2160) are a permutation of the digits of the original number (1260).

However, 126000 (which can be expressed as 21 × 6000 or 210 × 600) is not a vampire number, since although 126000 = 21 × 6000 and the digits (216000) are a permutation of the original number, the two factors 21 and 6000 do not have the correct number of digits. Furthermore, although 126000 = 210 × 600, both factors 210 and 600 have trailing zeroes.

The first few vampire numbers are:

: 1260 = 21 × 60
: 1395 = 15 × 93
: 1435 = 35 × 41
: 1530 = 30 × 51
: 1827 = 21 × 87
: 2187 = 27 × 81
: 6880 = 80 × 86
: 102510 = 201 × 510
: 104260 = 260 × 401
: 105210 = 210 × 501

The sequence of vampire numbers is:

:1260, 1395, 1435, 1530, 1827, 2187, 6880, 102510, 104260, 105210, 105264, 105750, 108135, 110758, 115672, 116725, 117067, 118440, 120600, 123354, 124483, 125248, 125433, 125460, 125500, ... {{OEIS|id=A014575}}

There are many known sequences of infinitely many vampire numbers following a pattern, such as:
: 1530 = 30 × 51, 150300 = 300 × 501, 15003000 = 3000 × 5001, ...

Al Sweigart calculated all the vampire numbers that have at most 10 digits.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sweigart |first1=Al |title=Vampire Numbers Visualized |url=http://coffeeghost.net/2011/07/19/vampire-numbers-visualized/}}</ref>

==Multiple fang pairs==
A vampire number can have multiple distinct pairs of fangs. The first of infinitely many vampire numbers with 2 pairs of fangs:

:125460 = 204 × 615 = 246 × 510

The first with 3 pairs of fangs:
:13078260 = 1620 × 8073 = 1863 × 7020 = 2070 × 6318

The first with 4 pairs of fangs:
:16758243290880 = 1982736 × 8452080 = 2123856 × 7890480 = 2751840 × 6089832 = 2817360 × 5948208

The first with 5 pairs of fangs:
:24959017348650 = 2947050 × 8469153 = 2949705 × 8461530 = 4125870 × 6049395 = 4129587 × 6043950 = 4230765 × 5899410

== Other bases ==

Vampire numbers also exist for bases other than base 10. For example, a vampire number in [[Duodecimal|base 12]] is 10392BA45768 = 105628 × BA3974, where A means ten and B means eleven. Another example in the same base is a vampire number with three fangs, 572164B9A830 = 8752 × 9346 × A0B1. An example with four fangs is 3715A6B89420 = 763 × 824 × 905 × B1A. In these examples, all 12 digits are used exactly once.
